To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
6-OHOA treatment has a marked inhibitory effect on both the IgG and IgM antibody responses to SRBC in CBA/J mice.

6-hydroxidopamine (6OHDA) treatment impairs humoral immune responsiveness in mice by decreasing the magnitude of the primary response to sheep red blood cell (SRBC) immunization, and by inhibiting immunological memory development.
depletion of catechols in the brain by 6-hydroydopamine impairs the humoral immune response by inhibiting the initiation of the primary immune response and immunological (memory) development.
In summary, our research is concerned with
elucidating the mechanisms by which the brain modulates the immune system.
the role of the nervous system in the control of the immune response and the mechanisms by which it exerts such control.

the effects of 1) brain catecholamine depletion on the immune response; 2) the role of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis in mediating the effects of 3) the effects of brain catecholaminergic depletion on the development of immunologic memory.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
depletion of brain NE impairs the primary antibody response, but not the secondary response or the memory response.
the impairment of humoral immunity in mice following 6-OHD treatment is the result of a central nervous system mediated immunosuppression.

the impairment of humoral immunity in 6-OHD-treated mice is due to an alteration in the central nervous system and not to the peripheral nervous system or to a direct effect of 6-OHD on lymphoid tissue.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the depletion of catechols from the brain by 6-OHD treatment has a profound effect on the immune system.
depletion of catechols in the central nervous system impairs both humoral and cell mediated immune responsiveness.
the catecholamines, NE and dopamine are involved in the initiation phase of the primary antibody responses and that the catechols are involved in immunological memory development.
The main takeaway from our work is that
catecholamines play a role in regulating immune responsiveness.
the brain plays an important role in the regulation of the immune response, and that this role is mediated by the central catecholamine systems.
catecholamine depletion in the brain has a profound inhibiting effect on the induction phase of the antibody response.
